utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All the accused are present, minus Vinko Pandurevic, who has sent a waiver which we have seen. Prosecution today is represented by Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, and Mr. Vanderpuye. Absent from the Defence teams I notice Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. Right. Yesterday we finished the witness off, General Simic. We admitted two documents offered by the Pandurevic Defence team, and we agreed, also, at the request of Mr. Josse to postpone the matter of documents to be tendered by others to today. I suggest -- propose to start with the list of documents of the Miletic Defence team that has been circulated. Is there any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection. Any of the other Defence teams wish to object to any of these documents? None. So all these documents are admitted. I'm just checking whether there are any that require translation. Yes, it's the last one, 5D1397, so that will be MFI'd pending translation thereof. Ms. Fauveau, I just want to make sure of something. In the list there was 5D1328 which, in the copy I have, has been crossed out with ink. It's the same -- all right. Okay. So you're not tendering that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, it's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I also have one document which the Gvero Defence team seeks to tender, and it's 6D311. Is there any objection, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that document is also admitted. And then there is a Prosecution list of nine documents, one of which will be under seal, that's 3938. Any objections, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. There are no objections. The only thing is could my colleague precesise [as interpreted] regarding 7D712, the list of prisoners in Batkovic, and we see the date 13th of May, does my colleague have any information as to whether this list was compiled on the date indicated 13th of May 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that reflects the date of transmittal by the authorities from the Republika Srpska pursuant to our RFA or the RFA of the requesting party. It's simply the first page that attaches the list. The list itself, as I understand it, is contemporaneous with the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And this is a Pandurevic document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is. I believe though, that we have used the document previously. I don't believe it had been tendered previously, but it is a document that all parties have previously used. Our exhibit number was 03939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one question, out of curiosity. I seem to remember Mr. Haynes yesterday, in mentioning the two documents, saying 712, amongst other things. 702? It's not the same one, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, these are different documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are different documents. Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With respect to our list, there is one other item that I believe we'll be in a position to offer tomorrow. I wanted to give my -- my learned friends an opportunity to look over the materials this evening. Madam Fauveau and I have been in consultation with respect to the tape recorded interviews of General Simic there. As the Court recalls there was some reluctance or hesitation on General Simic's part with respect to part of the interview. What we have agreed between the Miletic Defence team and the Prosecution is to offer to the Chamber the transcript pages from the 2004 and 2007 interviews which touch upon the conversation that General Simic testified about with General Miletic as well as the audio portion only of the section where the Prosecution cross-examined General Simic with respect to the guards about to kill the prisoners at the school. We would offer that for credibility purposes, if the Court is interested, to hear whether, in fact, that is on the tape. We do have the tape, and we can tender that portion, and we've agreed that -- between parties, that that can go to the Court if the Court desires to hear that specific portion of the tape which the Prosecution obviously alleges contains the statement by General Simic that one of his subordinates told him that when he arrived at the school the guards were about to execute those prisoners. But we've distributed the portions of the transcript to my friends pertinent the conversation that General Simic said he had with General Miletic for their review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Do you wish to comment on that, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I am fully in agreement with what the Prosecutor has said. I just want to be sure that all the parts of the interview relating to this issue are included in the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any -- thank you, ma'am. Any other comments from other Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, dealing with that first of all, we too would simply like to check what we have just been given. So I support what my learned friends have just said that that issue should be deferred until tomorrow. So far as the Prosecution list is concerned, we do have an objection to one document on that list, and that is P3938. The first issue that we would like to raise is why this document is being tendered under seal. We would invite a full explanation of that, both factual and legal, because we -- if it's admitted, we would much rather it was admitted publicly than under seal. But that's a discreet issue. So far as the admission of it is concerned, we are not inviting the Trial Chamber to prejudge the ongoing issue as to the admission of documents used by the Prosecution of Defence witnesses in the course of their cross-examination; though, I think, the filings in relation to that issue are closed or almost closed. Clearly the Trial Chamber has yet to make a determination. The Trial Chamber may have noted that the Gvero team have taken a particular stance in relation to that and accept for the most part that the Prosecution are entitled to introduce documents which go to the substance of any particular issue, in the course of their cross-examination. Putting it very shortly, Your Honours, we submit that this document crosses the line. We ask rhetorically why it was not introduced as part of the Prosecution case. We suggest that it's improper for it therefore to be introduced at this particular junction of the case, and in particular we suggest it's improper and unfair for it to be introduced via a witness called by a co-accused of our client; and the Trial Chamber will need to bear in mind the rules in relation to that. So bearing in mind all of those matters, we would invite the Court to refuse admission. We are quite content for the Chamber, if it so pleases to make a decision here and now. We are not asking for any decision to be deferred until the more general issue is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take the two issues, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First question of the confidentiality of this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may go into private session, for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now we are in open session and you need to comment on the rest of the observations, objections, made by Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as to the second grounds, the document clearly falls into the category of fair game for cross-examination. Like any other document that we've been using and that have been used by other parties, it has relevance and probative value in and of itself, and I won't belabour the position that we've taken in our filings on this issue; but it is no different than any other military record or other document that the Trial Chamber is -- has seen time and again. There is nothing unfair about it. The witness was called here. We had an opportunity to cross-examine, and the cross-examination was fair and appropriate; and it went directly to issues that my friends raised during the course of their examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the points made by Mr. Josse are the following, let's take them one by one. One is a rhetorical question: Why didn't you introduce this document in the course of your case -- case in chief. That's number one, you haven't touched on that. Second point made was a suggestion that it is improper for the Prosecution and unfair to have this document regarding General Gvero introduced via a witness called not by Mr. Gvero but by a co-accused. That's the second point made by Mr. Josse; and he suggested there are rules in relation to that, perhaps he can be more specific on that, on these rules, and you haven't touched on this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, in response to the rhetorical question, you know, we've got thousands and thousands of potential documents that -- that we could have introduced probative, we believe, of General Gvero's position, responsibilities; and ultimately his state of mind and a number of other issues that, for various reasons, we didn't introduce. It's as simple as that. I mean, I can't stand here and give the Court an explanation for all these documents. I don't know why this one in particular wasn't introduced during our case in chief, but we have an opportunity, my friends raised some very specific issues with respect to General Gvero; and I think it was fairly used and offered in response to those specific issues. As to the -- the second point, I don't see anything unfair about using a document when the Defence team for General Gvero engages in a long cross-examination of a witness and touches on kinds of issues. I just don't see anything in the rules that bars that or in the practice that we have engage in the two years for this trial that would bar that use. I don't see any prejudice that's been caused. I don't think there is any allegation of surprise, so I simply fail to see why it's unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If it helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We won't pursue the second point, certainly not at this juncture and we are not asking for a ruling on that. We most certainly will pursue the first point, and we submit that that isn't an adequate explanation; and the cross-examination that gave rise to the use of the document was nothing beyond what had been -- come out in the course of the Prosecution case in short; in other words, we weren't expanding the ambit of our case in any way at all. That's our submission, and therefore it should have been used as part of their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back into private session for on moment, please. I need to have you clarify something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision is, of course, without prejudice to the decision that we will handing later on on the motion and the responses that we've had and to which Mr. Josse referred to earlier on. Our decision on this particular document is first that it is a relevant question -- a relevant document, and essentially we allowed questions to be asked on the document, and there being no objection to those questions; and he answered those questions, we feel the need to have this document in the records if we are to understand and give weight to the whole testimony of General Simic. So the objection is overruled and as regards the status of this document, it will be admitted; and it will be preserved under seal. All right. We are going to have the next witness come in soon. Are there any submissions in relation to him before he is brought into the courtroom? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, this one is Milijanovic or -- or Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Pajic, okay. Thank you. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you're most welcome to this Tribunal. I am the Presiding Judge, my name is Agius. To my right I have Judge Kwon and Judge Stole, to my left Judge Prost. You have been summoned as a Defence witness by General Miletic. Before you start your testimony, you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic will be putting some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Pajic. Let me introduce myself to you officially. My name is Nenad Petrusic, as you know, and today I will be putting some questions to you on behalf of General Miletic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to speak more loudly and to approach the microphone as the interpreter cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, okay, you've heard the comment from the interpreter or not? You need to speak a little bit louder into the microphone, please. And I suggest you also tell your witness about the usual problem when counsel and witness speak the same language with the inevitable result of overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, before I officially -- before you officially introduce yourself, you've heard what the Presiding Judge has suggested. Given that we both speak the same language, you and I, too, naturally, have to wait before answering my questions. There is a monitor in front of you on which you can follow the transcript. Wait for the sentence to be completed, and then answer the question. You can follow this on the monitor. When taking the solemn declaration, I noticed that you spoke quite softly; so I would also like to ask you to feel free to speak a little more loudly. And now I would officially like to ask you to introduce yourself for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Velo Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of July, 1960, in Rogatica, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I completed primary school in Borike in 1975, and then I completed secondary military school, the communications section in Belgrade in 1979. It was within the land army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Have you completed any other military schools apart from this one?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, I graduated from the high military school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Having completed your secondary military school, did you receive a rank of any kind or did you find employment?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was promoted to sergeant, and I was sent to Sarajevo, military post 1519. My command was in Lukavica in Sarajevo, and I worked in the Konjic garrison. I worked on features for special purposes, Feature D.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what does that mean, Feature D?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Feature D, well, all features of special interest were exclusively features used to make calls, commands were located there, and communications equipment. Feature D -- well, the abbreviation used was D but in fact it was called Dilj. It was a military command post of the former presidency of the SFRY. It was a command post used under military or wartime, rather, conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I thought you said that this feature was called D; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dilj, D-I-L-J, Dilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of other such features or facilities in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, apart from these Dilj features, there were M features. Military command posts of the airforce on Jahorina, for example; and then Azlatice [phoen], the military command post of the former 7th army. Features G, Goljek [phoen], command post for the 7th army in Hans Pijesak. There were also radio relays, I won't list them, but there were such relays throughout the territories of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please speak up a bit and perhaps you could slow down when answering the questions. We're still discussing the feature or the facility Dilj, used for special purposes. Was it operational before the war?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the facility had been manned by people maintaining the facility, and it was in a state of readiness. It could receive men at any point in time, men intended -- or whose purpose was to work in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, how long did you stay in that facility?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the facility Dilj until the 9th of May 1992. The last two and a half months I spent there -- well, I had been cut off by the Muslims forces; and on the 9th of May 1992, a helicopter managed to withdraw us and transport us to Belgrade. In order to withdraw, we had to pass through the territory held by paramilitary units. We had to go to Bijelasnica, and then we were received and transported to the brigade command. The brigade command of the 398th brigade in Belgrade. Its headquarters were in Belgrade, and that's where we were transported to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to slow down for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, one moment. The interpreters, let me explain something, because, probably, you are not aware of how we operate here. What you say in the Serbian language is being simultaneously translated into English to us and into French to those of us that speak French. You're speaking a little bit too fast, so please slow down a little bit to enable the interpreters to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, did you stay on in the JNA after returning to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remained there until the 18th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After that day, did you at any point in time join the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 18th of May, we were transported from Belgrade to the Hans Pijesak section. I, in particular, was transported there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Which unit did you join in Hans Pijesak, could you tell us, briefly?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Hans Pijesak, or rather, to Crna Rijeka sector, I was received there by command of the 67th Communications Regiment, Colonel Miletic [as interpreted]; and the chief of the communications of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, Radomir Prole, was his name. I was appointed as command of the second platoon within the company. I was responsible for the communications garrison of the 67th Communications Regiment of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, let's just correct an error in the transcript. Was the commander of the 67th Communications Regiment Colonel Milikic [phoen]? What did you say? Who was Colonel Milikic?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was Colonel Milikic at the time, and one month later he went to Yugoslavia; and Lieutenant-Colonel Gordan Bosko [phoen] was appointed to that position. I am talking about May 1992. That's when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said you were appointed to a position in the 2nd platoon of the 67th Communications Regiment. Can you tell us how strong that platoon was?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the 2nd platoon within the company for the communications garrison. There were 25 men according to the establishment, but given the lack of men, I was alone in that platoon. I was the commander and I was also one of the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you mentioned a facility in Hans Pijesak, G1. We know this is an underground facility. Apart from that underground facility, were there any other military facilities in that area that is called Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that guilt, the G1 underground facility, there was a settlement, there were these cabins, these features that we used for offices from the Main Staff. And the feature, the facility, was for the 67th Communications Regiment. There was a facility for the 67th Communications Regiment also in the Crna Rijeka sector. There was another underground facility, Goljak 2, the so-called G1 facility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The so-called G2 facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was the command located in any of those cabins you have mentioned, the command of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The command was located in one of those cabins, the command of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. But that doesn't include the commander of the Main Staff who stayed in -- in a feature which was above ground within the G1 complex. It was the so-called Javor villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what were your duties? What tasks did you have, and in which facility did you perform your duties?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I performed my duties in the G1 facility, and my duties were to establish and maintain radio relay and wire communications for the needs of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We are now discussing 1995. So tell me, what kind of communications did the Main Staff use in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska mainly used radio relay communications and wire communications in 1995. When necessary, radio communications, but to a lesser extent. So these communications were used only when needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of your testimony, you also mentioned the -- a certain radio relay points. So what I am interested in is the following: Where were these radio relays located, radio relays used for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the points -- one of the main points used for the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army was at Veliki Zep. Then there were other sites on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there was Cer Strazbenice. Then we had Svinjar, Kozara, Klekovaca [phoen], Jahorina, Borasnica [phoen]; so I am talking about these sites, these communications points that we used for the communications needs of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska, and they had their subordinate units there. They had corps and there was the presidency of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the presidency, but with regard to the civilian institutions, were you linked up to any other institutions within Republika Srpska apart from the presidency?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We also had a communications network that was established with the government of the Republika Srpska with the Assembly and with the president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also said that you used radio relay and wire communications. My question has to do with radio relay communications. Could you briefly explain to us the way in which these communications function?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Radio relay devices are used by using a modulated signal which is conveyed or propagated throughout electro-magnetic waves to a receiver. In order to do this, in order to establish such communications, you need two radio relay devices. You need an optical line of sight; the distance must not exceed 50 kilometres. If one is to establish a viable communications link, you need to have a source of energy, and naturally you need to have a device with adequate frequency. This could be via the relay device, or they could be linked to the radio device by cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what about wire communications, how did that work?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Wire communications worked in the following way: You needed two participants being linked up by a low-frequency, a high-frequency cable. There had to be inductive phones being used, also, or a hand-carried switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in passing also radio communications, can you please tell us how that worked?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: RO2/2K, RUP-12, and radio telephones were the types of equipment most frequently used. Radio telephones that could be transported in vehicles, specifically. They use such frequencies as 30/70 megahertz. The radiation was a circular one, their antennas were not pointed any particular direction. These were used over short distances within optical line of sight that was open. The range being 10 to 15 kilometres with an optical line of sight available and open.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your experience, to what extent were these types of communication used by the Main Staff -- or, rather, at what levels of command were these types used? I am talking about radio communications.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Radio communications were hardly ever used by the Main Staff. Motorolas were used occasionally, but radio communications were hardly used at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the range of those Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Between 1 and 2 kilometres, depending on the lay of the land, depending on whether there was an optical line of sight with no repeaters involved. If there was a repeater, an intensifier, the range could easily have been increased with a repeater available, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you didn't have those repeaters, did you?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: No, not at Veliki Zep. Motorolas have to be used in direct communication, their range being between 1 and 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of equipment you used at the central communications hub out of Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: At Veliki Zep, there were a number of radio relay devices such as the SMC-1306B. FM-200 was another one, RRU800, RRU9B, RRU1. As for multiplex equipment for encoding speech, we used AMD310.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the underground facility itself, since you mentioned that particular piece of equipment with a transportable frequency. Were you using any other types of equipment there as well?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that underground facility, we also had -- well, as a matter of fact this was a device with transport or frequency, but we referred to them at a different way. They were these telephones. There was V120/341, VZ12K/24, VZ4/12, and an automatic telephone switchboard 80COM60, the capacity being 250 automatic numbers. Needless to say, they were automatic telephone devices inductor type or handheld type, M63, for example, inter-phones, mediation boards; and that was it as far as the telephone devices used at G1 were concerned. Perhaps I should also point out that the ones with portable frequency were interconnected by wire or by radio relay devices. The transmission was done by wire or by radio waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this abbreviation stands for, V120/3?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: This is a multiplex device with portable frequency. The circumference, within which it works is between 4 and 108 kilohertz. 120 means that it can convey 120 channels at the same time which means that you can have 120 lines of communication as it were operating through this device all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 5D139 [sic] brought up, thank you. My apologies, 5D1395. We can see zoom out a little in order to be able to see the entire page in a single screen. Thank you. That's quite efficient for our purposes, thank you. Can we please zoom out in order to get a view of the entire sheet. Thank you. I think that will do. Can I have the usher's assistance please, Madam Usher if you could please pass the electronic pen to Mr. Pajic so that he can enter certain changes to this chart or diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, Mr. Pajic, do you recognise the diagram in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It shows where the rooms were inside G1, inside this underground facility. It's a layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you the person who drew this diagram or plan?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the left upper corner, we see the date 19th of November 2008. Just below that date we see a signature, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this is the layout of G1, the underground facility, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to specifically explaining individual sections of this layout or ground plan, can you please tell me how much time you spent in this underground facility during your stint with the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: A total of nine years and ten months, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's proceed in the following way, sir. Let's go to this first room that says "the separation board." Can you see that writing in one of the rooms on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a number one there.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: There was an entrance, and then the rooms were 1A, 1B, 1C. 1B is the room you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So put the number on 1B, please.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the concept that I refer to as the separation board or switchboard?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: That's where all the wires are connected. All the cables are wider up as it were, as well as all the telephone and telegram cables, and they were all plugged into various devices. So they were all put together here, as it were, all the automatic numbers came from UM620, the switchboard. They went to the switchboard, the separation board, and all the cables that came from the cabins specifically from the Veliki Zep central communications hub and from the Hans Pijesak barracks. They were all put together and redirected, channeled over as it were here. And this device also made it possible for us to rearrange the different communication lines depending on the requirements placed on us by the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We have room 1B here. In addition to that room, we also see DS, a room marked as DS. Can you please place 1A there, the mark 1A. In addition, I would like you to please explain to us what the room was used for.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: This was a room with what we refer to as the mediation board. There was a handheld telephone switchboard there. There was an operator who would then switch the cables over, specifically automatic and direct lines depending on requirements. The established name was handheld telephone switchboard. Some people -- or hand-operated telephone switchboard. Some people called it the mediation board, but it was a hand-operated telephone switchboard and what was done there is certain channels and certain types of communications were rearranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next room is marked as ATCOM60. Put a number two there, please. As in the previous case, please explain what the room was used for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer, please, Mr. Pajic. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague, at line -- at page 23, I think it's line 12, it's -- it's a question that you put to the witness -- I'm sorry, it's line 2 where you refer to a room marked as DS. In the diagram that's provided in e-court, it seems to indicate PS, P like "pole." And I just wanted the record to be clear as to what we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, could we therefore go back to 1A, the initials that were placed there. Can you tell us what they read?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: In 1A we see the initials "PS," PS, which is short for "posraniski spor [phoen]." It was the device used to switch channels over between different kinds -- types of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the room marked as number 2.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: No, no need. Thank you. This is the automatic telephone switchboard, OM60. 250 automatic numbers being its capacity. This is a commutational system being used for direct communication by automatic selecting a number on a telephone device establishing communication between two participants. Therefore, the dialing itself was automatic and the numbers were automatic between two or more participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the following room as number 3.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Mark]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And tell us what UNF room means.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: In this room, there were telephone devices with portable frequency. As I mentioned before, these were V120/3, 12K/24, VZ4/12. These devices being connected by cable to the radio relay communications hub at Veliki Zep. They were used for demodulating signals from high frequency to low frequency, and then transmitting the signal to the end user.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next premise, could you mark it with a number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And it says "teleprinter station," so could you very briefly describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: In this room the telegraph devices are placed, teleprinters, PTL1 and PT100. They were used for the transmission of written information between two participants, and the room next to it, we can call it 4A; it was a workshop used for repairing these telegraph devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me be quite sure. Did you say that it was teleprinter PTL1, PTL1?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: ETL1, ETL1, Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next room, could you mark it with the number 5.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And it says STPL, SEKZS [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the abbreviation --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment please. There is an error here. The marking is STPL --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] STPL, that is the marking. SDKZC.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So could you please explain what the purpose of this room was?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an abbreviation which means crypto-protection or encoding station. It's a station for encoding. This is where acts were transformed into telegrams, telegrams coded, and sent as such to a particular participant. So in the teleprinter stations, documents were transformed into telegrams, encoded, and sent to participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next rooms, would you please mark them with the numbers 6, 7, and 8.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And tells what these rooms were used for.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: These rooms were intended for the rest of the personnel at the stationary communications centre, people working in the underground facility of the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the room at the top left hand corner, could you mark it too. Do you remember what number it bore?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And whose room was it?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: It was intended for the accommodation of the commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska in the event of danger from the air, chemical or biological threat or the incursion of enemy elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the room below the commander's, whose was that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: It was the number 9. It was for the same purpose only for the chief of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the next one please?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This was intended for the accommodation and stay of the chief of the sector for intelligence security affairs. Do you know who was the chief of staff of the army Republika Srpska in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of the army of Republika Srpska in 1995 was General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the chief of the sector for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The chief of the sector for intelligence and security was General Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next room, do you remember what number it bore?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it carried the number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And tell us what it was used for?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: It is the operations centre where the operations officer on duty would stay, and the officers working in the operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the room next to the operations room, you called it a working room --

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it with 12A.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: That was room number 13. It was a work room with maps or simply a kind of study for the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And we have three more rooms left. Could you mark them with the numbers 14, 15, and 16?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the next room, that is number 14, was envisaged to house the chief of the anti-air defences and airforce, the chief of the financial service, and for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. Pajic?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to room number 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I said the officers of the air force, anti-air defences, the officers of the financial service, and of the officers -- I can't exactly remember what these abbreviations stood for. I think for religious affairs or something like that. I forget what the precise name of the administration was for moral and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us now please, Mr. Pajic, whether all these rooms were linked by the communications system, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, all these premises were linked together by the communications system so that in each room there was an automatic telephone number that was forwarded from the automatic telephone exchange M60. So the cable linked all these premises and linked to the distribution board 1B.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the time that has passed, but also in view of the time you had spent in that underground facility, do you remember any telephone numbers?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Some of them, not all of them, but I do remember a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which numbers you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Let me start from room number 1 where it says telephone switching box 222 and 9; in number 2, 149; in number 3 -- in room number 3, 280; in room number 4, 221; in room number 10, 161 and 370; in room 9, 155 and 156; in room 12, 155 and 151; in room 13, 227; in room 15, 270. I can't remember the number in room 16. There are some numbers that I don't remember, but those I have indicated are quite right. I am quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember number 277?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Number 277, I think it was in room 13. I am not quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, could you tell us how - and on the basis of which principle - the number 155 functioned in view of the fact that we have them in two different places?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: This number, 155, was distributed into four different places and not two. In the underground facility, it was in room number 9 and room number 12. And at the same time, it was also distributed to the above-ground facilities, so-called Crna Rijeka, in the operations centre and in the premise where General Milovanovic rested and stayed. But when the operations centre and the chief were underground, then this number was switched off with plastic -- by a plastic device.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a leading question, but does that mean it would ring at the same time in room 9 and room 12?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It could ring in room number 9 and in room number 12. And technically, it's also possible to isolate room number 9 so that it would only ring in room number 12, but usually it would ring in both these rooms in view of the fact that it could be switched off on the inter-phones, so the alarm wouldn't go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, are you familiar with the concept of the command post in the rear?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know the command post in the rear. In -- the abbreviation was PKM. You are talking about the command post in the rear?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But before we go into that, could you tell me whether and how the premises of the command that were in the cabins, were they linked in the same way, and was the same system applied as in the underground facility?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The premises in the cabins or the settlement, as we called it, were also linked together; and each premises had an automatic 3 siphon number, because the underground cable linked the G1 underground facility with the above-ground facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in that facilities known as cabins, did they have the same devices as those in rooms from 1 to 5?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: These devices were not installed in the cabins if you're talking about those in rooms 1 to 5. In the cabins, there were only telephone receives, inductors, automatic ones, and inter-phones. F2 and F3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And before the break, could you tell us also how the rear command post was linked to the basic command post?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The command post in the rear, which was in the hotel in Hans Pijesak, was linked by cable - that is by wire - via the facility G2, the barracks in Hans Pijesak, the PTT - that is the post office - in Hans Pijesak, and the hotel where the command was situated. And we also had another relay direction, 0718; Veliki Zep, Hans Pijesak hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Petrusic, we'll soon be having the break any minute now. I suggest that the witness signs the document before the break. Mr. Pajic, you need to put your signature down below or upper right-hand corner, it's better -- okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Plus the date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Shall we have the break now? 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, we'll now carry on. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you still require the documents so that we bring it up if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, can you tell us how the basic command post was linked up to the rear command post in Hans Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The basic command post in Crna Rijeka was linked to the rear command post in Hans Pijesak by wire communications and by radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether these links or other words these numbers were three-figure numbers, or were other civilian numbers used?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers used were three-digit numbers sent from the switchboard to the rear command post via the relay post and via wire communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Where there devices for cryptographic protection, and was there a teleprinter at the rear command post?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the rear command post there was a coded teleprinter station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it also linked up to your teleprinter post?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Main Staff had teleprinter connections with all subordinate units, the corps, the PKMs, the rear command posts, the forward command posts; and they also had links to the presidency of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And now, very briefly what kind of direct links, if there were any such links, between the rear command post and the basic command post?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were direct links between the command post and the rear command post. There was a link between the encrypted teleprinter posts, and there were direct links between the duty officer at the PKM and the operations duty officer in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you aware of the fact that in the course of 1994 or 1995 forward command posts were established by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of 1994 a forward command post of the Main Staff was established in the sector. In fact, the name of the place was Jesenice. Prior to that act, a forward command post of the 93rd had been established on Jahorina for the Lukavac 93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This IKM, forward command post, in Jesenice, we heard something very briefly evidential about it, but do you know anything about the territory -- or, rather, the part of the Republika Srpska that it was located in?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: It was in the western part of Republika Srpska in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about which officers from the Main Staff were present at that IKM?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I remember that the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, was present at the IKM at the forward command post; and then there was Colonel Masal, and there were some other officers whose names I cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether when this IKM was established, the IKM -- whether the 67th Communications Regiment of the Main Staff had anything to do with the establishment of that post?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 67th Communications Regiment dealt with communications for the needs of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska. It was the command of the 67th Communications Regiment that provided the equipment and men for the IKM in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say "equipment," what do you have mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Well, if a unit located in the area before the IKM was set up had certain equipment we could use, for example, relay devices or frequency carrier, well then in such cases we wouldn't establish new networks. We would use the channels in existence, and if there was anything missing, we would add the necessary equipment. We had an FM20 [as interpreted] radio relay that was set up, and crypto-protection station that was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line -- rather, page 33, line 12, it says FM20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that you said an FM200; can you confirm whether we are dealing with an FM200 device?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the device is an FM200 device.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when this was being done, when the communications network was being set up, what kind of direct links were there to the basic command post and the forward command post, if there were any such links in the western part of the Republika Srpska; or, rather, I am talking about the IKM in Jesenice?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The forward command post was linked to the command post via relay communications. There were four channels. There was a direct link between the command of the Main Staff and General Milovanovic at the forward command post. There was a link between the operations duty officer and the duty officer at the IKM, and then there was a link -- or there was a communications network for forwarding written information, the teleprinter post was used for these purposes, and there was a fourth channel that was used to make sure that one had an automatic three-digit number at the IKM. So, when you say "three-digit number," I am thinking about the M60 device, and this is how information was sent to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to correct something -- or, rather, clarify something. When you spoke about direct links between the IKM and the Main Staff, can you tell us whether General Milovanovic and General Mladic had a direct link?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had a direct link.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me - and this is a subject we will go back to later - was the link you've been discussing protected, encrypted, link?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, these links were secure links.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And does that involve all the four channels that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Well, usually channels used for the commander -- for the operations centre, would be secure. But it wasn't necessary to secure the link that was used to forward information to the teleprinter post, and the three-digit number that was at the IKM was also a secure link at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's briefly go back to the telephone number 155. Does this -- was it possible to transfer this telephone number from Crna Rijeka to the IKM?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was technically possible to transfer it; however, at the time it wasn't transferred to the IKM. All I can remember is that it was transferred in 1993, there was an IKM at Jahorina, but in 1995 there was some other number that was used. Not the one you have mentioned. But technically, it is possible to move or, rather, transfer that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, and you said that in 1995 this number had not been transferred?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: No, it hadn't been transferred at that point in time. It was used at the IKM in Jesenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, given the duties you had to perform, given your position, and given the devices that you worked with, do you know whether the communications of the army of Republika Srpska could be tapped?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: It was technically possible to wire-tap these communications. Devices that used high frequencies, for example, the SMC1306B, was a device that could be wire-tapped only with a lot of difficulty. As far as the FM200 device is concerned, I am talking about relay devices that used a frequency of 610 to 960, well, if they -- if these devices were secured then they couldn't be wire-tapped. So technically, it was possible to wire-tap the communications system, but it was very complicated. The devices have to be used at maximum output. It's possible to have an intermediary station between the electro-magnetic waive length. You have to have two radio devices. You have to have two MF devices for one of the participants or both of the participants; so you practically have to enter the area where the relay system is being used in order to tap into it. Or, you have to set up a station opposed for both participants; in such a case, you can only wire-tap communications in one direction. So technically this was possible, but it was very difficult. But when I mentioned secured links, I said that it wasn't possible to wire-tap them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff have secure communications links?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army had secured links to all subordinate units, to corps; it had a secure link to the government, the Assembly, and the president of the Republika Srpska; and it also had a secure link to the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, do you exclude the possibility of the ABiH wire-tapping these devices or some other act?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to these communications links, as I have already said, it wasn't possible to wire-tap them. I am talking about secure links, about this secure communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Two radio relay devices have often been mentioned here. One radio relay device in the so-called RRU1, I am interested whether when this device was used to establish communications, was it possible to intercept these communications?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The RRU1 radio relay device is a one-channel device. Its range is up to 30 kilometres. If there is an optical line of sight -- if there is a good optical line of sight. And given that its antenna isn't a directional one, it's not as focused, and it uses lower frequencies; so it is possible to intercept communications when this device is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what is your experience with the 800 radio relay device?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: RRU800 is one of the radio relay devices. It is a somewhat older model, the range being 690 [as interpreted] to 960, same as the 200, and the 9B. As I explained, it can't be intercepted. From one of the two relay posts communicating, if it operates at its full capacity, it normally admits a rather powerful magnetic field. Or, for example, it can go into a node with one of the posts involved in the communication, but I am not aware of this ever happening. I apologise, 610 to 960. I see that it was mis-recorded, the frequency range of the RRU is 610 to 960 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat yet again. What is the frequency range for that device, RRU800?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: The range is between 610 and 960 megahertz, and there are another two device that have the same range, the 200 and the RRU9B; I keep repeating that. But the thing is all these three radio devices use the same frequency range, and the frequency range is 610 to 960 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, this being the case, one could in theory listen to one participant at a time, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, as long as the party doing the intercepting is actually located behind one of these posts if they are receiving a reflected way or through an antenna. Thus is set up at the point of reception. In that case, he would be able to listen to one of the parties involved in the exchange. In order to hear both ends of the communication, you would need to interpose a post within the electro-magnetic sheathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the interposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't want to interrupt my colleague before the long, but I did just want to let the Court know that this is an area of examination of which we've had no prior notice, and I wanted to let -- well, rather, ask the Court's permission when I cross-examine this witness it may take longer than I had initially anticipated and this relates to intercepts and the capability to receive and transmit them, which we've gone over I think rather extensively in the case; but still think I will need to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I saw Madam Fauveau even nodding. Yes, we'll see into that later, and you tell us what your needs are and we'll decide depending on what we consider to be in the best interests of justice at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, you are right, but my understanding is that these are general questions on intercepting without going into detail. Anyway, I was about to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, after completing your training and education you got a promotion, you were now a sergeant and you dealt with communications, generally speaking. Throughout your career in wartime or before the war broke out, were you ever trained in encryption, to perform jobs that had to do with encryption?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took a course in encryption, in cryptographic protection, if you like. At various points throughout my career I used devices for the encryption of speech. I was required to take and complete that course, and the course applied to both encryption of both written material and voice encryption. However, I never actually performed the job of an encryption officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P192.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, in your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to repeat what he just said, to speak up, and to move closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the interpreters couldn't hear what you were saying. So if you could repeat the question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, do you distinguish in your profession between what you normally refer to as an act or enactment, on the one hand, and a telegram on the other?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is something that we refer to as an act or a document and then there is a telegram, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You can see a document that is now being displayed on the monitor in front of you. It's in the Latinic script. Can you tell us what it shows?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: This document was intended to be an act or a document; however, it really is nothing. It's certainly not an act. An act should display in its header, in the upper left corner the name of the relevant institution or unit, the file number, the date it was sent, the addressee, the substance of the document, and finally the sender. There should be a handwritten signature and a round stamp. This document bears none of the above; therefore, I can hardly refer to it as a telegram or, indeed, an act.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If you look at the right-hand side, towards the bottom in the Cyrillic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can please pull up the English a little, page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If you look at the Cyrillic it reads, "Handed over at 1510, 13th of July 1995." And then there is a signature. Can you comment on this, what the document says?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: It tells me nothing. If we are talking about what the regulations said, this is not done properly. I happen to know this lad, Darko Gojkovic. He noted down the time, who it was sent to. I really don't know. I don't know if the recipient ever in fact received this. It is not confirmed on the face of the document. It was done improperly. This is not an act, and it's certainly not a telegram that was sent. Maybe it was sent at some point, but being what it is, it was done improperly; and I don't think it could have been accepted by the encryption system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So how far do you think this document could possibly have got?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Believe me I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, its doesn't matter. So yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 5D1005.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, this is a document from the Drina Corps command. Can you please have a look and read through it.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the encryption people at the Main Staff, did you comply with the rules on official correspondence and on encryption throughout 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we complied. And this is one of the documents or; rather, orders by the Drina Corps done in that spirit. So this was the way it was supposed to be done, and we certainly complied with the rules and regulations on encryption in our office work. This order shows nothing new. All it is is some sort of a warning to comply with the rules in the way just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P183.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document and tell me, if you can, whether this is an act or a telegram as defined a while ago.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Again, it is neither. The only difference between this document and the previous one being this one was actually typewritten using a -- an ATL1 teleprinter; nevertheless, what's missing here is a rectangular stamp showing the time of deliver, the time the telegram was processed, and likewise there is no confirmation of receipt by the other end. In the right upper corner we have a time. There should be a signature. This is probably the encryption officer same as in the previous document, but I really can't say. So again, what we have here is one of those improper telegrams. I am not saying that it wasn't sent. Mind you, it may I have been sent in this shape and form; all I am saying is that it was not done properly not in keeping with the rules, and we see no confirmation of the other end or the other side receiving the document. Therefore, we don't know if the addressee, the intended recipient ever received the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Petrusic. Just to have things clear in our mind and that -- so that at all times we will be on the same wavelength. You've drawn a distinction between an act and a telegram. I think we understand quite well what a telegram is. In order to avoid any possibility of not understanding you, what do you really mean by "act"? And then please make sure that the witness agrees with the meaning of "act" or the definition of "act" as you will be giving it to us. What do you understand by "act"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word "act" is anything in writing, typewritten, signed, by a sender showing a stamp and, of course, a header indicating the name of the command sending the document. I think the witness himself in part has explained this from the perspective of his own profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The important thing is that you and the witness in using the descriptive word "act" mean exactly the same thing. That's what we want to know. Mr. Pajic, you've just heard Mr. Petrusic explain to us what, in his mind, he means when he uses the word "act." Is this what you understand by the word "act" yourself, or do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree with Mr. Petrusic. The only thing is when such an act arrives at the teleprinter station for encryption, the encrypting officer receives this and then puts a rectangular stamp on it. He also notes the time, records the time on the face of the document, after which the document is returned to whoever the sender happens to be. A telegram is what is sent to the opposite side as it were. It is first encrypted and then one uses a teleprinter post to send it along, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, to clear any doubts, we talked about the rules and office work, the document being 5D1994 -- 11, rather, 1194. Page 9 of that document, please. In the English version it is also page 9. Let us see Provision 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, please look at this paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version move on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question is: Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is this what is called an act, does this define an act according to your professional terminology and the terminology of office work that you used in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in the e-court is page 15, and in the Serbian version --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would you please read, for yourself, paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Under the concept of "telegram," do you mean precisely what is stated here in paragraph 36?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back to document P183.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Will you please read through this telegram. It's quite brief.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: First of all let me ask you whether in July 1995 you were in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in that period in G1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you were ever included in the plan of work of the communications centre, this radio device 2/2 K and KZU-63?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I do not remember at all such an order nor did we form such a radio network, RU 2/2. It was not formed for the needs of the above-indicated institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see document 5D1020.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before we discuss this document, let me ask you: Do you remember whether the Main Staff ever used a radio device 2/2 K?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: No. It never used that device RU 2/2 K.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Will you please read through this document as well.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would it happen that communications would be switched off in the Main Staff in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Before I say that, I would like to say that this is how a telegram sent and received properly should look like. There is a rectangular stamp, the time it was received, stamped by the receiver in the Main Staff; and that is how a telegram properly received should look like. As for this order, it would happen in the course of the war that there was an interruption in the communications because of failure in the generators which were outdated, low voltage strength of the network, a shortage of fuel, and it happened during the bombing that we would switch off the facility during day-time because of the danger from the air. In view of the fact that when the devices got switched on, they radiate through the antennas and they reveal the location of the radio stations. So there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of cases at lower tactical levels of interruptions in the communications system?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems at other facilities, especially where the nodes and centres were improvised due to the same causes, a shortage of fuel, a breakdown in the generators. This would happen quite frequently that the frequencies would breakdown, and it would be impossible to communicate telegrams and other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more document, please. 5D1019. In the Serbian version, please scroll the document down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My first question, Mr. Pajic, is: Do you consider this to be a correct regular telegram or act or document?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a proper act prepared to be sent as such from the encryption teleprinter station as a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I should like you to focus your attention on the last sentence before point 2. It says -- it begins with the word "note."

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Obviously there are problems in telecommunications, so it is impossible to send a report. How long would these failures last, are you aware?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: That depended on the cause, whether it is a radio relay device, the source of energy; it could last from five minutes to a whole day sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there were such failures at the Veliki Zep --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't you think he has already answered this question, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll move on to the very end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, did you know Mr. Miletic?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: I did know General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he spent any time in the underground facility in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Miletic did stay in the underground part of the facility G1, sometimes -- some time around the 25th of May when there was the bombing of the Jahorina stream, when the operations centre was moved underground; that is, to room number 12. And that is where I would see General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know where his family was staying?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: His family, as far as I know, was living in Belgrade. They had an apartment in Belgrade, and that is where his wife and children were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether he went to visit his family?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, like all the other officers there was a monthly schedule for their visits to families; and, therefore, General Miletic went to visit his family as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether the General visited his family in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC
utterances.text: There is an event that I remember quite well. On the 11th of July 1995, in a weekend settlement in Hans Pijesak, we had a grill. We were roasting a lamb, and this was organised by Mr. Petrovic; and this ended in the afternoon and mostly the officers from the rear command post, we sat at a table. And next to me Colonel Simovic, Mirko, was sitting. And he asked, Where is Mica? And Petrovic responded, Which Mica? And then he said, Miletic.
